newsitem.title: USA: Early winter U.S. Northwest snowpack looks strong.
newsitem.headline: Early winter U.S. Northwest snowpack looks strong.

text.p: Hydropower generation in the U.S. Northwest has been near average for the water year which began October 1, but early signs indicate above-average snowpack, according to industry experts.
The Northwest has already seen a rash of heavy storms this winter, but sources emphasize most of the recent rainfall has been on the eastern side of the Cascade Mountains.
"We have been hit with front after front and waves of rain," said Cindy Hendrickson, chief of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' reservoir control center in Portland, Ore.
But the above-average precipitation has not had much impact on Columbia and Snake River flows, with the smaller Willamette River taking the brunt of flooding, she noted.
Another cold front is expected to hit the area this week.
The Corps of Engineers, which operates most of the massive federal hydroelectric projects in the region, has drawn down reservoirs at the Grand Coulee dam on the Columbia as a precaution.
The measures were taken, "in case we need to protect Portland harbor at the confluence of the Willamette and Columbia," Hendrickson said.

A power management source at Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), which markets electricity produced at federal dams in the Northwest, also said recent storm patterns mainly affect power generation if the federal system is backed down for flood control purposes.
In November, however, flows on the Snake River did rise as rain melted some lower elevation snow and the extra water moved through the dam system.

Official statistics for average precipitation during November are not yet available, but an hydrologist at the Northwest River Forecast Center in Portland said Tuesday the Columbia Basin average looks roughly in line with October's 131 percent of normal average volumes.
Hendrickson at the Army Corps of Engineers noted the storms have "built up snowpack," which could spell high runoff volumes next spring.
The first official snowpack measurements are made in January, but industry sources say accumulation at higher elevations began earlier than usual this year and November's storms added to it.
The BPA source also said higher-elevation snowpack on the eastern and northern Cascade Mountains "is working real well so far," indicating ample snowmelt in the spring.

"I am bullish on the market until the first snow surveys come out," said a trader at a Northwest utility. "It is just a guess, but I think prices will come down when people see volumes even higher than last year's."
